title: T1566.003 — Phishing - Spearphishing via Service
subtitle: Watch how an attacker rents a legitimate platform and turns its trust against the victim.
aria: Animated diagram of a spearphishing via service attack: the attacker signs up to a legitimate file-sharing service, uploads a weaponized document, the service emails the victim from its real domain, the victim downloads and opens the file, and malware calls back to the attacker. A full written description of every step follows below the canvas.

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: The threat actor. They sign up to the legitimate service and control the lure content and the command-and-control server.

nodes.label: Cloud Service
nodes.tip: A genuine file-sharing or e-signature service. It is not malicious itself; it is being abused. Its notification emails are real and well signed.

nodes.label: Email Gateway
nodes.tip: The company mail security service. It trusts the service's domain, so this message usually passes all checks.

nodes.label: Attacker C2
nodes.tip: The attacker's command-and-control server. Malware on the victim's machine connects here after execution.

nodes.label: User Mailbox
nodes.tip: The targeted employee's mailbox. The service notification arrives next to legitimate ones.

nodes.label: User Endpoint
nodes.tip: The victim's computer. The download is clean by network standards; the danger appears only when the document runs.

nodes.label: SOC / Defender
nodes.tip: The security operations center. It needs mail, proxy, endpoint, and SaaS audit logs to see the whole chain.

steps.title: Create the account
steps.caption: the attacker signs up to the legitimate file-sharing service with a disposable mailbox and a persona shaped like a known vendor or colleague.
steps.defender: Ask your SaaS vendors for abuse-report contacts and know their audit sharing options. You cannot see account creation on their side, so the relationship must exist before an incident.

detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Build the lure
steps.caption: a weaponized document named like real business correspondence is uploaded, and a public share link is created without password protection.
steps.defender: When you later investigate, ask the provider for the sharing account details. Public links with business-looking names are the signature of this abuse.

steps.title: The service emails the victim
steps.caption: the platform sends its standard notification from its real domain. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all pass because the sender is genuine.
steps.defender: Do not trust a message just because the sending platform is real. Extract the sharing user and compare it with your known contacts and vendors.

steps.title: The victim opens the notification
steps.caption: the message sits next to legitimate service mails, carries no attachment, and the victim clicks through to view the shared document.
steps.defender: Alert on first-ever sender-recipient combinations inside trusted SaaS domains, and make the report button work for service notifications too.

steps.title: Download from a trusted host
steps.caption: the document downloads from the sanctioned SaaS domain. Proxy logs show an ordinary business download; the file lands on disk with a Mark of the Web.
steps.defender: Log downloads by user even for sanctioned domains. The filename, size, and content type give the trail context when an endpoint alert arrives minutes later.

steps.title: The payload executes
steps.caption: the victim opens the document and enables editing. The macro spawns a script interpreter which calls back to the attacker's server.
steps.defender: Your strongest endpoint signal: an Office application acting as the parent of wscript, cmd, or mshta. Alert on the process tree, not just the download.

detection.label: Partial signal
detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: Attacker takes control
steps.caption: the attacker drives the implant interactively, harvesting credentials and mapping the network, while the share link and SaaS account stay live for reuse.
steps.defender: Remember the delivery account: ask the provider to suspend it and pull the share audit trail, so reuse of the same lure is stopped for other targets too.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Defender responds
steps.caption: the SOC correlates mail, download, and process-tree signals, isolates the host, revokes the share via the provider, and ships a new detection for Office spawning script hosts.
steps.defender: Turn the incident into coverage: the joined chain (sanctioned SaaS mail + download + hostile process tree) is exactly the correlation your SIEM should now automate.
